q: You have a DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity. During peak hours, you experience throttling. Which approach will NOT help resolve this?

opts.d: Use exponential backoff in your application

exp.a: Auto Scaling can dynamically adjust capacity to handle peak loads.
exp.b: On-Demand mode automatically handles any traffic level without throttling.
exp.c: Adding LSIs does not resolve throttling; in fact, LSIs share capacity with the base table and can worsen the issue.
exp.d: Exponential backoff is a recommended retry strategy to handle throttled requests gracefully.

q: A DynamoDB table uses a composite primary key. Which statement is TRUE?

opts.a: The partition key must be unique across all items
opts.b: The combination of partition key and sort key must be unique
opts.c: The sort key must be unique across all items
opts.d: Neither key needs to be unique

exp.a: With a composite key, multiple items can share the same partition key as long as sort keys differ.
exp.b: In a composite primary key, the combination of partition key and sort key must be unique for each item.
exp.c: Sort keys do not need to be globally unique; they must be unique within a partition key.
exp.d: The combination of both keys must be unique to identify each item.

q: Which DynamoDB feature should you use if you need to replicate data across 3 AWS regions for a globally distributed application?

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams captures changes but doesn't automatically replicate across regions.
exp.b: DynamoDB Global Tables provides fully managed multi-region, multi-active replication across multiple AWS regions.
exp.c: DAX is an in-memory cache within a single region, not for cross-region replication.
exp.d: PITR is for backup and recovery, not cross-region replication.

q: What is required to enable DynamoDB Global Tables?

opts.b: The table must use provisioned capacity
opts.d: The table must have at least one GSI

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams must be enabled with the 'New and old images' stream view type for Global Tables to function.
exp.b: Global Tables work with both provisioned and on-demand capacity modes.
exp.c: DAX is not required for Global Tables.
exp.d: GSIs are not required for Global Tables.

q: You need to calculate the RCUs required for 50 strongly consistent reads per second, with each item being 6 KB. How many RCUs do you need?

exp.a: 50 RCU would only cover items up to 4 KB each.
exp.b: 75 RCU is incorrect; the calculation yields a different result.
exp.c: 6 KB / 4 KB = 1.5, rounded up to 2 RCUs per read. 50 reads × 2 RCU = 100 RCUs.
exp.d: 150 RCU is more than needed for this scenario.

q: You need 80 eventually consistent reads per second for items of 12 KB each. How many RCUs are required?

exp.a: 80 RCU does not account for the item size exceeding 4 KB.
exp.b: 12 KB / 4 KB = 3 RCUs for strongly consistent. For eventually consistent: 3 / 2 = 1.5 RCU per read. 80 × 1.5 = 120 RCUs.
exp.c: 160 RCU would be for strongly consistent reads, not eventually consistent.
exp.d: 240 RCU is double what is needed.

q: You need 100 writes per second for items of 2.5 KB each. How many WCUs are required?

exp.a: 100 WCU only covers 1 KB items.
exp.b: 200 WCU is insufficient for 2.5 KB items.
exp.c: 250 WCU is incorrect; 2.5 KB rounds up to 3 KB.
exp.d: 2.5 KB rounds up to 3 KB. 3 KB / 1 KB = 3 WCUs per write. 100 × 3 = 300 WCUs.

q: You need 200 transactional writes per second for items of 2 KB each. How many WCUs are required?

exp.a: 200 WCU does not account for item size or transactional overhead.
exp.b: 400 WCU only accounts for item size (2 WCU per item) but not transactional overhead.
exp.c: 600 WCU is incorrect.
exp.d: 2 KB / 1 KB = 2 WCUs per write. Transactional writes cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 WCUs per transactional write. 200 × 4 = 800 WCUs.

q: Which DynamoDB Streams view type captures both the old and new images of the item?

exp.a: KEYS_ONLY captures only the key attributes of the modified item.
exp.b: NEW_IMAGE captures only the new version of the item after modification.
exp.c: OLD_IMAGE captures only the old version of the item before modification.
exp.d: NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES captures both the old and new versions of the item, useful for comparing changes.

q: How many DynamoDB Streams view types are available?

exp.a: 2 is incorrect; there are more view types available.
exp.b: 3 is incorrect; there are 4 stream view types.
exp.c: There are 4 stream view types: KEYS_ONLY, NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE, and NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES.
exp.d: 5 is incorrect; DynamoDB Streams has exactly 4 view types.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid DynamoDB data type?

exp.a: String (S) is a valid scalar data type in DynamoDB.
exp.b: Number (N) is a valid scalar data type in DynamoDB that covers integers and floats.
exp.c: Float is not a separate DynamoDB data type; floating-point values are stored as Number (N) type.
exp.d: Binary (B) is a valid scalar data type in DynamoDB.

q: What is the purpose of DynamoDB Contributor Insights?

opts.b: To identify the most frequently accessed and throttled items in a table

exp.a: Encryption at rest is a separate feature, not Contributor Insights.
exp.b: DynamoDB Contributor Insights identifies the most accessed and throttled keys, helping diagnose hot key issues.
exp.c: Backups are handled by on-demand backup and PITR features.
exp.d: Global replication is handled by Global Tables.

q: Which API operation is used to create a DynamoDB table?

exp.a: PutTable is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.
exp.b: CreateTable is the correct DynamoDB API operation to create a new table.
exp.c: NewTable is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.
exp.d: InsertTable is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.

q: What happens when a DynamoDB item's TTL timestamp expires?

opts.b: The item is typically deleted within 48 hours of expiration
opts.c: The item is moved to cold storage

exp.a: TTL deletion is not immediate; it's a background process.
exp.b: DynamoDB TTL typically deletes expired items within 48 hours of the expiration time. Items may still appear in reads until actually deleted.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not move items to cold storage via TTL.
exp.d: Items do not become read-only; they are eventually deleted.

q: Does DynamoDB TTL consume write capacity when deleting expired items?

opts.a: Yes, it consumes WCUs from provisioned capacity
opts.b: No, TTL deletions do not consume any provisioned throughput
opts.c: Yes, but at a reduced rate

exp.a: TTL deletions are free and do not consume provisioned WCUs.
exp.b: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items in a background process at no cost and without consuming provisioned throughput.
exp.c: TTL deletions are completely free regardless of capacity mode.
exp.d: TTL deletions are free in both provisioned and on-demand modes.

q: Which index type shares throughput capacity with the base table in DynamoDB?

exp.a: GSIs have their own independent provisioned throughput separate from the base table.
exp.b: LSIs share the provisioned throughput (RCUs and WCUs) with the base table.
exp.c: Only LSIs share throughput with the base table; GSIs have separate capacity.
exp.d: LSIs do share throughput with the base table.

q: Which statement about GSIs is TRUE?

opts.a: GSIs must have the same partition key as the base table
opts.b: GSIs can have a different partition key and sort key from the base table
opts.c: GSIs only support strongly consistent reads
opts.d: GSIs share WCUs with the base table

exp.a: GSIs can have a completely different partition key from the base table.
exp.b: GSIs can have any attribute as the partition key and sort key, different from the base table's primary key.
exp.c: GSIs only support eventually consistent reads, not strongly consistent.
exp.d: GSIs have their own provisioned throughput, independent of the base table.

q: Which type of read consistency is supported by Global Secondary Indexes?

opts.c: Both strongly and eventually consistent reads

exp.a: GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads.
exp.b: Global Secondary Indexes only support eventually consistent reads.
exp.c: Only eventually consistent reads are supported on GSIs; strongly consistent reads are not available.
exp.d: Transactional reads are not specific to GSIs.

q: Which type of read consistency is supported by Local Secondary Indexes?

opts.c: Both strongly and eventually consistent reads

exp.a: LSIs support more than just eventually consistent reads.
exp.b: LSIs support more than just strongly consistent reads.
exp.c: Local Secondary Indexes support both strongly consistent and eventually consistent reads.
exp.d: LSIs do support read operations with both consistency options.

q: What is the storage limit for a partition key value (including all its items) in a table with Local Secondary Indexes?

exp.a: 5 GB is incorrect; the limit is 10 GB per partition key value when LSIs are present.
exp.b: When LSIs are defined, all items with the same partition key (across the table and its LSIs) are limited to 10 GB total.
exp.c: 20 GB exceeds the partition key value collection size limit.
exp.d: There is a 10 GB limit per partition key value collection when LSIs are used.

q: What is the maximum size of data returned by a single BatchGetItem call?

exp.a: 1 MB is the limit for a single Query or Scan call, not BatchGetItem.
exp.b: 4 MB is the size limit for transactions, not BatchGetItem.
exp.c: A single BatchGetItem call can return up to 16 MB of data.
exp.d: 64 MB exceeds the BatchGetItem data limit.

q: What is the maximum total data size for a DynamoDB transaction (TransactWriteItems or TransactGetItems)?

exp.a: 1 MB is the limit for Query/Scan results, not transactions.
exp.b: DynamoDB transactions are limited to 4 MB of data in total across all items in the transaction.
exp.c: 16 MB is the limit for BatchGetItem, not transactions.
exp.d: 25 MB is not a DynamoDB limit.

q: Which feature allows you to import data from Amazon S3 into a new DynamoDB table?

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams is for capturing changes, not importing data.
exp.b: DynamoDB Import from S3 allows you to import data from S3 into a new DynamoDB table without writing code or managing infrastructure.
exp.c: AWS Data Pipeline can be used but is not the native DynamoDB import feature.
exp.d: DAX is a caching layer, not an import feature.

q: Which formats are supported for DynamoDB Import from S3?

opts.a: CSV, DynamoDB JSON, and Amazon Ion

exp.a: DynamoDB Import from S3 supports CSV, DynamoDB JSON, and Amazon Ion formats.
exp.b: CSV is one of the supported formats, but not the only one.
exp.c: JSON is one of the supported formats, but not the only one.
exp.d: Parquet and Avro are not supported formats for DynamoDB Import.

q: What happens when a GSI's provisioned write capacity is exceeded?

opts.b: Writes to the base table are throttled
opts.d: The base table switches to on-demand mode

exp.a: The effect is not limited to GSI queries only.
exp.b: When a GSI's write capacity is throttled, the base table writes are also throttled because DynamoDB must keep the GSI in sync with the table.
exp.c: GSIs are never automatically deleted due to throttling.
exp.d: The table does not automatically switch capacity modes.

q: Which DynamoDB operation allows you to delete multiple items in a single API call?

exp.a: DeleteItems is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.
exp.b: BatchWriteItem supports both PutRequest and DeleteRequest, allowing you to delete up to 25 items in a single call.
exp.c: BulkDelete is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.
exp.d: RemoveItems is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.

q: What is the purpose of the FilterExpression in a DynamoDB Query?

opts.a: It determines which partition to read from
opts.b: It filters results AFTER the query has consumed read capacity
opts.c: It reduces the read capacity consumed
opts.d: It specifies the sort key condition

exp.a: The partition to read from is determined by KeyConditionExpression, not FilterExpression.
exp.b: FilterExpression is applied AFTER items are read from the table. It does not reduce RCU consumption; it only filters the returned results.
exp.c: FilterExpression does NOT reduce read capacity; items are still read and capacity is consumed before filtering.
exp.d: Sort key conditions are specified in KeyConditionExpression, not FilterExpression.

q: Which AWS service can be used to migrate data from a relational database to DynamoDB?

exp.a: AWS DMS supports migration from relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, etc.) to DynamoDB.
exp.b: CloudFormation is for infrastructure provisioning, not data migration.
exp.c: AWS Config is for compliance monitoring, not data migration.
exp.d: Amazon Inspector is a security assessment service, not a migration tool.

q: Which DynamoDB capacity mode is more cost-effective for predictable, steady workloads?

opts.b: Provisioned capacity mode with reserved capacity

exp.a: On-Demand mode is more expensive per request for steady, predictable workloads.
exp.b: Provisioned capacity with reserved capacity offers significant cost savings (up to 77%) for predictable workloads.
exp.c: They do not cost the same; provisioned is cheaper for steady workloads.
exp.d: DAX is a separate caching feature; On-Demand with DAX would still be more expensive for steady workloads.

q: How often can you switch between DynamoDB provisioned and on-demand capacity modes?

exp.a: Once per day is close but not the precise AWS term.
exp.b: You can switch between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes once every 24 hours.
exp.c: Switching is not unlimited; there is a 24-hour cooldown.
exp.d: Once per week is incorrect; you can switch every 24 hours.

q: What does DynamoDB use to distribute data across partitions?

opts.b: Internal hash function applied to the partition key

exp.a: The sort key is not hashed for partition distribution.
exp.b: DynamoDB uses an internal hash function on the partition key value to determine which physical partition stores the data.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not use round-robin; it uses deterministic hash-based distribution.
exp.d: Distribution is deterministic based on the partition key hash, not random.

q: What is the Optimistic Locking strategy in DynamoDB?

opts.a: Locking the entire table during writes
opts.b: Using a version number attribute with conditional writes
opts.c: Using DynamoDB Streams to prevent conflicts

exp.a: DynamoDB does not support table-level locking.
exp.b: Optimistic locking uses a version number attribute and ConditionExpression to ensure items haven't changed between read and write operations.
exp.c: DynamoDB Streams captures changes but doesn't directly prevent conflicts.
exp.d: Encryption is unrelated to concurrency control.

q: Which DynamoDB write operation creates an item if it doesn't exist or completely replaces it if it does?

exp.a: UpdateItem modifies existing attributes or adds new attributes without replacing the entire item.
exp.b: PutItem creates a new item or completely replaces an existing item with the same primary key.
exp.c: BatchWriteItem uses PutItem internally but is for batch operations.
exp.d: CreateItem is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.

q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a DynamoDB DAX cluster?

exp.a: 5 nodes is below the maximum DAX cluster size.
exp.b: 10 nodes is below the maximum DAX cluster size.
exp.c: A DynamoDB DAX cluster can have a maximum of 11 nodes (1 primary + 10 read replicas).
exp.d: 15 exceeds the maximum DAX cluster node count.

q: DAX is compatible with which DynamoDB API calls?

opts.c: Only read operations with no write-through

exp.a: DAX supports more read operations than just GetItem and Query.
exp.b: DAX supports GetItem, BatchGetItem, Query, and Scan for reads, and also supports write-through for PutItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem, and BatchWriteItem.
exp.c: DAX supports both read caching and write-through operations.
exp.d: DAX does not handle management operations like CreateTable.

q: What is the default TTL for items in the DAX item cache?

exp.a: 1 minute is not the default DAX item cache TTL.
exp.b: The default TTL for the DAX item cache is 5 minutes.
exp.c: 10 minutes is not the default DAX item cache TTL.
exp.d: 30 minutes is not the default DAX item cache TTL.

q: Which caches does DAX maintain?

opts.d: Item cache, query cache, and write cache

exp.a: DAX maintains more than just the item cache.
exp.b: DAX maintains more than just the query cache.
exp.c: DAX maintains two caches: an item cache (for GetItem/BatchGetItem) and a query cache (for Query/Scan results).
exp.d: DAX does write-through but does not maintain a separate write cache.

q: You have a table with 20 GB of data and experience uneven access patterns. Which strategy helps distribute load?

opts.a: Add a random suffix to the partition key (write sharding)

exp.a: Write sharding by adding a random suffix to partition keys distributes data and traffic across more partitions.
exp.b: Increasing item size does not help distribute load across partitions.
exp.c: Adding LSIs does not solve uneven data distribution.
exp.d: Reducing attributes doesn't address partition-level access distribution.

q: What is the maximum number of projected attributes in a DynamoDB secondary index?

exp.a: 10 is incorrect; more attributes can be projected.
exp.b: 20 is the number of GSIs allowed, not projected attributes.
exp.c: You can project up to 100 non-key attributes into a secondary index when using INCLUDE projection type.
exp.d: There is a limit of 100 non-key projected attributes (when using INCLUDE).

q: What are the three projection types available for DynamoDB secondary indexes?

exp.a: The three projection types are ALL (all attributes), KEYS_ONLY (only key attributes), and INCLUDE (specific non-key attributes).
exp.b: FULL, PARTIAL, NONE are not valid DynamoDB projection type names.
exp.c: ALL, SOME, NONE are not the correct DynamoDB projection type names.
exp.d: COMPLETE, KEYS, SELECTED are not valid projection type names.

q: What is a DynamoDB partition key also commonly called?

exp.a: Primary key can refer to either partition key alone or partition key + sort key combination.
exp.b: The partition key is also known as the hash key because DynamoDB uses a hash function on it for data distribution.
exp.c: Range key is another name for the sort key, not the partition key.
exp.d: Foreign keys are a relational database concept not used in DynamoDB.

q: What is a DynamoDB sort key also commonly called?

exp.a: Hash key is another name for the partition key, not the sort key.
exp.b: Partition key is the first component of the primary key, not the sort key.
exp.c: The sort key is also known as the range key because it allows range queries on items with the same partition key.
exp.d: Index key is not a specific DynamoDB term for the sort key.

q: Which service can you use with DynamoDB Streams to build a search index in Amazon OpenSearch?

exp.a: S3 is a storage service and cannot process DynamoDB Streams directly.
exp.b: AWS Lambda can process DynamoDB Streams events and push data to Amazon OpenSearch to build a search index.
exp.c: RDS is a relational database and not used for processing streams.
exp.d: CloudFormation is for infrastructure provisioning, not stream processing.

q: Which DynamoDB operation supports optimistic concurrency control?

exp.a: Scan with FilterExpression is for reading and filtering data, not concurrency control.
exp.b: UpdateItem with ConditionExpression enables optimistic concurrency by checking conditions (like version number) before writing.
exp.c: Query with ProjectionExpression is for read operations, not concurrency control.
exp.d: BatchGetItem is a read operation and doesn't support conditional logic.

q: What is the maximum size of a DynamoDB reserved capacity purchase term?

exp.a: 6 months is not a valid DynamoDB reserved capacity term.
exp.b: DynamoDB reserved capacity can be purchased for 1-year or 3-year terms with significant cost savings.
exp.c: 5 years is not a valid DynamoDB reserved capacity term.
exp.d: Monthly is not a valid reserved capacity term.

q: What is the maximum discount available with DynamoDB reserved capacity (3-year term)?

exp.a: 50% is less than the maximum available discount.
exp.b: 60% is less than the maximum available discount.
exp.c: DynamoDB reserved capacity offers up to 77% savings with a 3-year term compared to on-demand pricing.
exp.d: 90% exceeds the maximum discount available for DynamoDB reserved capacity.

q: Which AWS service provides a serverless SQL query capability to analyze DynamoDB exported data in S3?

exp.a: Amazon Athena can query DynamoDB data exported to S3 using standard SQL without managing any infrastructure.
exp.b: RDS is a managed relational database, not for analyzing S3 data.
exp.c: DynamoDB itself doesn't provide SQL analytics on exported data.
exp.d: ElastiCache is an in-memory caching service, not for SQL analytics.

q: What is the WCU cost of a transactional write for a 1.5 KB item?

exp.a: 1 WCU doesn't account for rounding up or transactional overhead.
exp.b: 2 WCU accounts for item size (1.5 rounds to 2) but not transactional overhead.
exp.c: 3 WCU is incorrect.
exp.d: 1.5 KB rounds up to 2 KB = 2 WCUs. Transactional writes cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 WCUs.

q: What is the RCU cost of a transactional read for a 6 KB item?

exp.a: 2 RCU is the cost for a strongly consistent read of 6 KB, not transactional.
exp.b: 3 RCU is incorrect.
exp.c: 6 KB / 4 KB = 1.5, rounded up to 2 RCUs for strongly consistent. Transactional reads cost 2x, so 2 × 2 = 4 RCUs.
exp.d: 6 RCU is more than needed for a transactional read of 6 KB.

q: Which DynamoDB table class is designed for infrequently accessed data?

exp.a: DynamoDB Standard is the default class for frequently accessed data.
exp.b: DynamoDB Standard-IA offers lower storage costs (up to 60% less) for tables with infrequent access patterns.
exp.c: There is no DynamoDB Glacier class; Glacier is an S3 storage class.
exp.d: There is no DynamoDB Archive class.

q: How much storage cost savings does DynamoDB Standard-IA provide compared to Standard?

exp.a: 30% is less than the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.
exp.b: DynamoDB Standard-IA offers up to 60% lower storage costs compared to the Standard table class.
exp.c: 80% exceeds the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.
exp.d: 90% exceeds the actual savings offered by Standard-IA.

q: What is the minimum capacity for DynamoDB Auto Scaling target?

exp.a: 0 is not valid; you must have at least 1 unit of capacity.
exp.b: The minimum provisioned capacity you can set is 1 RCU and 1 WCU.
exp.c: 5 is not the minimum; it can be set lower.
exp.d: 10 is not the minimum; capacity can go as low as 1.

q: Which service provides change data capture (CDC) functionality for DynamoDB?

exp.a: Kinesis Data Firehose is for data delivery, not change data capture from DynamoDB.
exp.b: DynamoDB Streams provides change data capture (CDC) by recording item-level changes in near real-time.
exp.c: SQS is a message queue service, not specifically for DynamoDB CDC.
exp.d: SNS is a notification service, not for change data capture.

q: Can DynamoDB Streams data be sent to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams?

opts.a: No, they are completely separate services
opts.b: Yes, through Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB feature

exp.a: DynamoDB does support sending change data to Kinesis Data Streams.
exp.b: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB allows you to capture item-level changes and send them to a Kinesis data stream with longer retention (up to 365 days).
exp.c: While Lambda can bridge the two, there is a native feature for this.
exp.d: Glue is not required; there is a native integration.

q: What is the maximum retention period when using Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB?

exp.a: 24 hours is the DynamoDB Streams retention, not Kinesis Data Streams.
exp.b: 7 days is the default Kinesis retention, but extended retention is available.
exp.c: 30 days is less than the maximum available retention.
exp.d: Kinesis Data Streams supports up to 365 days of data retention.

q: Which DynamoDB feature allows conditional deletes?

exp.a: TTL automatically deletes expired items based on timestamp, not conditions on attributes.
exp.b: DeleteItem with ConditionExpression allows you to delete an item only if specified conditions are met.
exp.c: BatchWriteItem supports delete operations but does NOT support ConditionExpressions.
exp.d: Scan reads data; it does not delete items.

q: What is the maximum number of attributes that can be defined as key schema elements (partition key + sort key) for a DynamoDB table?

exp.a: 1 attribute is for a simple primary key (partition key only), but composite keys use 2.
exp.b: A DynamoDB table key schema can have at most 2 attributes: one partition key and one optional sort key.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not support 3 key attributes in the table schema.
exp.d: 5 attributes cannot be part of the table's key schema.

q: What happens when you perform a Scan operation with a Limit parameter set to 10?

opts.a: It returns exactly 10 items matching filter criteria
opts.b: It evaluates 10 items and returns those that match any filter
opts.c: It scans the entire table and returns the first 10 results

exp.a: Limit doesn't guarantee 10 matching items; it limits how many items are evaluated.
exp.b: The Limit parameter controls how many items DynamoDB evaluates (not returns). If a FilterExpression is applied, fewer items may be returned.
exp.c: With Limit set to 10, DynamoDB evaluates only 10 items, not the entire table.
exp.d: Using Limit is a valid operation and does not throw an error.

q: Which DynamoDB feature enables you to perform read and write operations on encrypted data without decrypting it first?

opts.a: Client-side encryption with DynamoDB Encryption Client

exp.a: The DynamoDB Encryption Client provides client-side encryption, allowing you to encrypt specific attributes before storing them.
exp.b: Server-side encryption is transparent and handled by AWS; you don't interact with encrypted data directly.
exp.c: VPC Endpoints control network routing, not encryption.
exp.d: IAM policies control access permissions, not encryption of data.

q: You need to store session data that expires after 24 hours. Which DynamoDB feature is most appropriate?

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams is for capturing changes, not expiring data.
exp.b: DynamoDB TTL is ideal for session management; set the expiration timestamp 24 hours from creation and items are automatically deleted.
exp.c: DAX is a caching layer and doesn't handle data expiration.
exp.d: Global Tables is for multi-region replication, not data expiration.

q: Which DynamoDB limit applies to the number of attributes in a key schema across all LSIs and the base table?

exp.a: Across the table and all its LSIs, you can have a maximum of 5 different attributes defined as keys (since LSIs share the partition key and each has its own sort key).
exp.b: 10 is incorrect; the limit is 5.
exp.c: There is a limit on key attributes.
exp.d: 25 is the BatchWriteItem limit, not related to key attributes.

q: What is Parallel Scan in DynamoDB?

opts.b: Dividing a table into segments and scanning them concurrently
opts.c: Using multiple DAX nodes for reads

exp.a: Parallel Scan is specific to Scan operations, not queries.
exp.b: Parallel Scan divides the table into segments and allows multiple workers to scan different segments simultaneously, improving throughput.
exp.c: DAX nodes are for caching, not parallel scanning.
exp.d: Parallel Scan works on a single table divided into segments, not multiple tables.

q: Which AWS service can be used to visualize DynamoDB metrics and set alarms?

exp.a: Amazon CloudWatch provides metrics, dashboards, and alarms for DynamoDB including consumed capacity, throttled requests, and latency.
exp.b: X-Ray is for distributed tracing of application requests, not specifically for DynamoDB metrics.
exp.c: CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing, not for visualizing operational metrics.
exp.d: AWS Config tracks configuration changes, not operational metrics.

q: Which CloudWatch metric indicates that DynamoDB requests are being throttled?

exp.a: ConsumedReadCapacityUnits shows capacity used but not throttling.
exp.b: ThrottledRequests metric shows the number of requests that exceeded the provisioned throughput limits.
exp.c: SuccessfulRequestLatency measures response time, not throttling.
exp.d: SystemErrors indicates internal DynamoDB errors, not throttling.

q: What happens when you delete a DynamoDB table?

opts.a: Only the data is deleted; the table structure remains
opts.b: The table, all items, all LSIs, and all GSIs are permanently deleted
opts.c: The table is moved to a recycle bin for 30 days
opts.d: Only GSIs are deleted; the base table remains

exp.a: Deleting a table removes everything, not just data.
exp.b: When you delete a DynamoDB table, the table, all items, all local and global secondary indexes are permanently and irreversibly deleted.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not have a recycle bin; deletion is permanent.
exp.d: The entire table and all associated indexes are deleted.

q: Which DynamoDB operation can modify multiple attributes of an existing item without replacing the entire item?

exp.a: PutItem replaces the entire item; it does not selectively modify attributes.
exp.b: UpdateItem allows you to add, modify, or remove individual attributes of an existing item without affecting other attributes.
exp.c: BatchWriteItem only supports PutItem and DeleteItem, not partial updates.
exp.d: ReplaceItem is not a valid DynamoDB API operation.

q: You need to store items larger than 400 KB in DynamoDB. What is the recommended approach?

opts.a: Compress the item to fit within 400 KB
opts.b: Store the large data in S3 and save the S3 object URL in DynamoDB
opts.c: Split the item into multiple DynamoDB items
opts.d: All of the above are valid approaches

exp.a: Compression is one valid approach if it brings the size under 400 KB.
exp.b: Storing large objects in S3 with a reference in DynamoDB is the most common pattern for large data.
exp.c: Splitting items across multiple DynamoDB items with the same partition key is also a valid approach.
exp.d: All three approaches are valid strategies for handling data larger than 400 KB in DynamoDB.

q: What is the maximum number of DynamoDB tables that can participate in a single Global Table?

exp.a: Global Tables are not limited to just 2 regions.
exp.b: 5 regions is not the limit for Global Tables.
exp.c: DynamoDB Global Tables can replicate across all available AWS regions where DynamoDB is available.
exp.d: 10 regions is not a hard limit; Global Tables support all DynamoDB regions.
